message.content:
The sea had been Elias’s only companion for thirty years. Its voice was a constant, a low growl against the granite cliffs, a hiss on the shingle. Tonight, the wind was a sharp knife, and the waves threw themselves at the lighthouse base with a desperate fury.

After the storm passed, a bruised dawn revealed the wreckage. Kelp, splintered wood, and a single, glinting bottle lay half-buried in the sand. Elias, his joints aching, retrieved it. The cork was stubborn, sealed with wax. Inside, a single sheet of paper, yellowed and brittle.

The handwriting was a woman’s, elegant and fading. *“To whoever finds this,”* it began. *“My name is Clara. I am not lost at sea. I am lost in a life that feels like a ship with no rudder. I am writing this from my bedroom window, watching the same lighthouse you now tend. I see its light every night, a promise of something steady. I am afraid I am becoming a ghost in my own home. If you find this, know that your light has been the only thing that has kept me tethered to hope.”*

Elias read it three times. He knew every house in the small coastal town below. He knew the lonely widow in the grey cottage, the one who never came to the market. He looked at the lighthouse, at the great lens that had just spent the night battling the storm.

He didn’t know her name, but he knew her fear. He took a fresh piece of paper, dipped his pen in ink, and wrote: *“Clara. The light is always on. And so am I. The kettle is always hot. Come for tea. – Elias.”* He sealed it in a new bottle and, with a prayer to the sea, cast it back into the waves, hoping the tide would be kinder this time.
